title: Strategy Implementation and Evaluation
outcomes: Choose structures and align culture with strategy.
Explain strategic leadership, change and digital transformation.
Apply strategic control types and performance measures.

meta.exam_tip: Link each implementation tool to a fact in the case — structure, culture, leadership or control.

concepts.title: From formulation to implementation
body: Strategy formulation decides what to do; implementation turns plans into action through structure, resources, policies, systems, leadership and culture. Good formulation fails without effective implementation, and vice versa.

Implementation tasks: building an organisation capable of execution, allocating resources to strategy-critical activities, setting supportive policies, installing information and reward systems, and leading change.
Formulation is mostly analytical and done by a few top managers; implementation is operational and involves the whole organisation.
concepts.analogy: A brilliant strategy on paper is worthless until people and systems act on it.
concepts.work: A bank deciding to go digital must retrain staff, change branch roles and invest in IT — that is implementation.

concepts.title: Structure and culture
body: Structure (the "hard" side) follows strategy: functional (by function, suits single-product firms), divisional (by product, region or customer), matrix (dual reporting for projects), SBU (grouping related businesses), network or virtual (outsourced partners), and hourglass (fewer middle levels, enabled by technology).
Culture (the "soft" side) is the shared values, beliefs and norms that shape behaviour; a strategy-supportive culture eases implementation, while a mismatched culture resists change.
Leaders align structure and culture with strategy through communication, role models, rewards and selection.
concepts.analogy: Structure says who does what; culture decides how willingly they do it.
concepts.work: A conservative, rule-bound culture struggles to execute a fast-innovation strategy.

concepts.title: Strategic leadership and change, including digital transformation
body: Strategic leadership provides vision, builds commitment and manages change. Transformational leaders inspire change and innovation; transactional leaders work through rewards and established systems — each suits different situations.
Kurt Lewin's change model: unfreezing (making people ready for change), changing (introducing new behaviours and systems) and refreezing (making the new ways stable).

Digital transformation uses technologies such as cloud, analytics, automation and AI to change business models, processes and customer experiences; it needs leadership support, new skills, data governance and attention to cyber risks.
concepts.analogy: Change sticks only when people are prepared, supported and the new way is locked in.
concepts.work: A retailer adopting app-based ordering trains staff, revises incentives and phases out old processes.

concepts.title: Strategic control and performance measures
body: Control types: operational (individual tasks — stock, quality, cost), management (overall resource use in departments), and strategic (whether the strategy is being implemented as planned and delivering intended results).

Strategic control types: premise control (checks assumptions), strategic surveillance (broad, unfocused monitoring), special alert control (rapid response to sudden events) and implementation control (milestones and step-wise review).

Strategic performance measures track progress on financial and non-financial dimensions — e.g. the balanced scorecard's financial, customer, internal process and learning-and-growth perspectives — along with benchmarking against best performers.
concepts.analogy: Control closes the loop: are we doing what we planned, and is it working?
concepts.work: Customer retention and employee skills are as important to track as profit.

illustrations.title: Choosing a structure
illustrations.q: Suggest a suitable organisation structure for each and give a reason: (a) a single-product start-up with 40 staff; (b) a company selling FMCG, paints and pharma; (c) an engineering firm running several large client projects that need specialists from many departments; (d) a group with dozens of businesses that wants each unit to plan like an independent company.

head: Case
Structure
Reason
rows: Simple, specialised departments; efficient for one product
Each division focuses on its own market and is accountable for results
Project managers and functional heads share authority, pooling specialists across projects
Related businesses grouped into units with their own strategy and profit responsibility
solution.title: Organisation structures

illustrations.title: Is the strategy still on track?
illustrations.q: An airline's strategy assumed stable fuel prices and steady business travel. Explain how each type of strategic control would help: premise control, strategic surveillance, special alert control and implementation control.

head: Control
How it helps the airline
rows: Tracks key assumptions — fuel prices, business-travel demand — and flags when they no longer hold
Broad scanning of news, trends and industry developments for unexpected threats
Rapid, crisis-team response to sudden events such as a pandemic or a major accident
Checks milestones — new routes launched, cost targets met — and decides whether to continue or adjust
solution.title: Strategic control

jobs.title: Implementation roadmap
jobs.situation: A manufacturer has decided to enter export markets.
steps: Define structural changes, such as an export division.
Plan communication and training for change.
jobs.takeaway: Every strategic decision needs an owner, a budget, a timeline and a measure.

options: An analytical task of a few planners
mcqs.explain: Implementation involves people and systems across the organisation. In practice: needs leadership.

mcqs.q: A structure with dual reporting to project and functional managers is:
mcqs.explain: Matrix structures combine project and functional lines. In practice: risk of conflicting authority.
Structure is hard; culture is soft. In practice: both must fit strategy.

mcqs.q: In Lewin's model, making new behaviours stable is:
mcqs.explain: Refreezing locks in the change. In practice: through rewards and policies.
mcqs.topic: Strategic leadership and change, including digital transformation

mcqs.q: Checking whether planning assumptions are still valid is:
mcqs.explain: Premise control monitors key environmental and industry assumptions. In practice: focus on critical premises.

mcqs.q: A rapid response to a sudden crisis is handled by:
mcqs.explain: Special alert control uses crisis teams for unexpected events. In practice: pandemic response.

mcqs.q: The balanced scorecard includes which perspective?
mcqs.explain: It covers financial, customer, internal process and learning-and-growth perspectives. In practice: links strategy to measures.

mcqs.q: A leader who inspires followers to pursue a new vision is:
mcqs.explain: Transformational leaders drive change through inspiration. In practice: suited to turbulent environments.
mcqs.topic: Strategic leadership and change, including digital transformation

summary: Structures: functional, divisional, matrix, SBU, network, hourglass.
Culture aligns behaviour; leadership drives change.
Lewin: unfreeze, change, refreeze; digital transformation.
Controls: premise, surveillance, special alert, implementation; balanced scorecard.
traps: Surveillance is broad; premise control is focused on assumptions.

viva.q: How do formulation and implementation differ?
viva.model: Formulation decides what to do through analysis by top managers; implementation puts it into action through people, structure and systems across the organisation.
Grouping related divisions into strategic business units, each with its own strategy, managers and profit responsibility.
Unfreezing prepares people for change, changing introduces new ways, and refreezing makes them stable.
A broad, unfocused monitoring of many information sources to detect unexpected developments affecting strategy.

viva.q: Name the four balanced scorecard perspectives.
viva.model: Financial, customer, internal business process, and learning and growth.

cases.title: NovaBank goes digital
cases.case: NovaBank decides to move most services online. Branch staff fear job losses; the bank is organised by region with many management layers; the CEO holds town halls to explain the vision; a sudden cyber-attack disrupts services for a day.

mcqs.q: The CEO's town halls mainly support:
mcqs.explain: Explaining the need for change prepares people. In practice: address fears openly.
mcqs.topic: Strategic leadership and change, including digital transformation

mcqs.q: Reducing management layers with technology moves the bank towards:
mcqs.explain: Hourglass structures shrink middle management through IT. In practice: redeploy staff.

mcqs.q: Responding to the cyber-attack calls for:
mcqs.explain: A sudden crisis needs rapid, planned response. In practice: crisis teams and backup systems.

mcqs.q: This change is an example of:
mcqs.explain: Using technology to change processes and customer experience. In practice: needs new skills and cyber security.
mcqs.topic: Strategic leadership and change, including digital transformation
